ns9:Group.ns9:description: It is important to ensure adequate logging of mail server connections so as to support detecting any unauthorized activity.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Enable Mail Server Logging
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: To ensure logging is enabled, perform the following command: grep "mail\." /etc/syslog.conf The output received should indicate either mail.crit or mail.*.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: If informational and more severe SMTP service messages are not logged, malicious activity on the system may go unnoticed.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure Mail Server Logging Level
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: If sendmail is installed, perform the following checks: Edit the file /etc/mail/sendmail.cf and confirm that the following line appears: O LogLevel=9 If postfix is installed, this check is not applicable.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: If Sendmail is not configured to log at level 9, system logs may not contain the information necessary for tracking unauthorized use of the sendmail service.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Mail Server Features
ns9:Group.ns9:description:
Mail servers are used to send and receive email over the network. Mail is a very common service, and Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs) are obvious targets of network attack. Ensure that machines are not running MTAs unnecessarily, and configure needed MTAs as defensively as possible.
Very few systems at any site should be configured to directly receive email over the network. Users should instead use mail client programs to retrieve email from a central server that supports protocols such as IMAP or POP3. However, it is normal for most systems to be independently capable of sending email, for instance so that cron jobs can report output to an administrator. Most MTAs, including Postfix, support a submission-only mode in which mail can be sent from the local system to a central site MTA (or directly delivered to a local account), but the system still cannot receive mail directly over a network.
The alternatives program in Red Hat Enterprise Linux permits selection of other mail server software (such as Sendmail), but Postfix is the default and is preferred. Postfix was coded with security in mind and can also be more effectively contained by SELinux as its modular design has resulted in separate processes performing specific actions. More information is available on its website, http://www.postfix.org.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Disable Debug Command
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: From a terminal, type the following commands: # telnet localhost 25 # debug If debug is disabled, one of the following errors should be returned: 500 error code of "command unrecognised" 550 error code of "access denied"
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Debug mode is a feature present in older versions of sendmail which, if not disabled, may allow an attacker to gain access to a system through the sendmail service.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Disable Decode Command
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Edit the file(s) /etc/aliases and /usr/lib/aliases, if either exist, to ensure that the decode: and uudecode: entries do NOT include the file path to uudecode, such as the following: decode: |/usr/bin/uudecode uudecode: |/usr/bin/uuencode -d
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: A common configuration for older Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs) is to include an alias for the decode user. All mail sent to this user is sent to the uudecode program, which automatically converts and stores files. By sending mail to the decode or the uudecode aliases present on some systems, a remote attacker may be able to create or overwrite files on the remote host. This could possibly be used to gain remote access.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Disable EXPN Command
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: If sendmail is installed, perform the following checks: Edit the file /etc/mail/sendmail.cf to ensure that the following PrivacyOptions line appears and includes noexpn: O PrivacyOptions=authwarnings,novrfy,noexpn,restrictqrun If postfix is installed, this check is not applicable.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The SMTP EXPN function allows an attacker to determine if an account exists on a system, providing significant assistance to a brute force attack on user accounts. EXPN may also provide additional information concerning users on the system, such as the full names of account owners.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Disable Help Command
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: If sendmail is installed, perform the following checks: Edit the file /etc/mail/helpfile to ensure that the file is empty. If postfix is installed, this check is not applicable.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The HELP command should be disabled to mask version information. The version of the SMTP service software could be used by attackers to target vulnerabilities present in specific software versions.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Disable VRFY Command
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: If sendmail is installed, perform the following checks: Edit the file /etc/mail/sendmail.cf to ensure that the following PrivacyOptions line appears and includes novrfy: O PrivacyOptions=authwarnings,novrfy,noexpn,restrictqrun If postfix is installed, this check is not applicable.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The VRFY command allows an attacker to determine if an account exists on a system, providing significant assistance to a brute force attack on user accounts. VRFY may provide additional information about users on the system, such as the full names of account owners.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Disable WIZ Command
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: From a terminal, type the following commands: # telnet localhost 25 # wiz If wiz is disabled, the following error should be returned: 500 error code of "command unrecognised"
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Very old installations of the Sendmail mailing system contained a feature whereby a remote user connecting to the SMTP port can enter the WIZ command and be given an interactive shell with root privileges.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Don't Display Version
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: If sendmail is installed, perform the following checks: Edit the file /etc/mail/sendmail.cf to ensure that the following SmtpGreetingMessage line does not appear as: O SmtpGreetingMessage=$j Sendmail $v/$Z; $b If the above line appears, it should be changed to: O SmtpGreetingMessage= Mail Server Ready ; $b If postfix is installed, perform the following checks: Edit the file /etc/postfix/main.cf to ensure that the following smtpd_banner line does not appear with $mail_version. If so, remove the $mail_version entry or comment out the entire line to use the default value.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The version of the SMTP service can be used by attackers to plan an attack based on vulnerabilities present in the specific version.
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: SENDMAIL_CONFIG=$(rpm -ql sendmail | grep sendmail.cf) SENDMAIL_MAINCONF=$(rpm -ql sendmail | grep sendmail.mc) if [ "$(rpm -q sendmail-cf &>/dev/null; echo $?)" = "0" ]; then if [ -e "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}" ]; then if [ "$(grep -c "^define(\`confSMTP_LOGIN_MSG" "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}")" = "0" ]; then sed -i "0,/^define/s/\(^define\)/define(\`confSMTP_LOGIN_MSG', \` Mail Server Ready ; $b')dnl\n\1/" "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}" elif [ "$(grep -c "^define(\`confSMTP_LOGIN_MSG', \` Mail Server Ready ; \$b')dnl" "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}")" = "0" ]; then sed -i "s/^define(\`confSMTP_LOGIN_MSG.*/define(\`confSMTP_LOGIN_MSG', \`Mail Server Ready ; \$b')dnl/" "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}" fi m4 "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}" > "${SENDMAIL_CONFIG}" fi else sed -i 's/O SmtpGreetingMessage=.*/O SmtpGreetingMessage= Mail Server Ready ; $b/' "${SENDMAIL_CONFIG}" fi service sendmail restart 1>/dev/null

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Restrict Mail Forwarding
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: If sendmail is installed, perform the following checks: Edit the file /etc/mail/sendmail.cf to ensure that the following ForwardPath line appears without any file path specified: 0 ForwardPath Perform a search on the system for any .forward files by issuing the following command: # find / -name .forward The above command should not return any results. If so, delete each file returned.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The .forward file allows users to automatically forward mail to another system. Use of .forward files could allow the unauthorized forwarding of mail and could potentially create mail loops which could degrade system performance.
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: SENDMAIL_CONFIG=$(rpm -ql sendmail | grep sendmail.cf) SENDMAIL_MAINCONF=$(rpm -ql sendmail | grep sendmail.mc) if [ "$(rpm -q sendmail-cf &>/dev/null; echo $?)" = "0" ]; then if [ -e "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}" ]; then if [ "$(grep -c 'confFORWARD_PATH' "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}")" = "0" ]; then sed -i "0,/^define/s/\(^define\)/define(\`confFORWARD_PATH',\`')dnl\n\1/" "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}" elif [ "$(grep -c "define(\`confFORWARD_PATH',\`')dnl" "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}")" = "0" ]; then sed -i "s/define(\`confFORWARD.*/define(\`confFORWARD_PATH',\`')dnl/" "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}" fi m4 "${SENDMAIL_MAINCONF}" > "${SENDMAIL_CONFIG}" fi else sed -i 's/O ForwardPath.*/O ForwardPath/' "${SENDMAIL_CONFIG}" fi service sendmail restart 1>/dev/null for FILE in $(find /etc -name .forward -type f 2>/dev/null); do rm -f ${FILE} done

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Restrict Mail Relaying
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: If sendmail is installed, perform the following checks: Edit the file /etc/mail/sendmail.cf to ensure that only the following DaemonPortOptions line appears: O DaemonPortOptions=Port=smtp,Addr=127.0.0.1, Name=MTA Edit the file /etc/mail/sendmail.mc to ensure that the following promiscuous_relay line does NOT appear: promiscuous_relay If postfix is installed, perform the following checks: Edit the file /etc/postfix/main.cf to ensure that only the following inet_interfaces line appears: inet_interfaces = localhost Edit the file /etc/postfix/main.cf to ensure that only the following smtpd_client_restrictions line appears: smtpd_client_restrictions = reject
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: If unrestricted mail relaying is permitted, unauthorized senders could use this host as a mail relay for the purpose of sending SPAM or other unauthorized activity.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: LDAP
ns9:Group.ns9:description: LDAP is a popular directory service, that is, a standardized way of looking up information from a central database. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 5 includes software that enables a system to act as both an LDAP client and server.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Configure OpenLDAP Clients
ns9:Group.ns9:description: This section provides information on which security settings are important to configure in OpenLDAP clients by manually editing the appropriate configuration files. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 5 provides an automated configuration tool called authconfig and a graphical wrapper for authconfig called system-config-authentication. However, these tools do not provide as much control over configuration as manual editing of configuration files. The authconfig tools do not allow you to specify locations of SSL certificate files, which is useful when trying to use SSL cleanly across several protocols. Installation and configuration of OpenLDAP on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 5 is available at https://access.redhat.com/site/documentation/en-US/Red_Hat_Enterprise_Linux/5/html/Deployment_Guide/ch-ldap.html.
ns9:Group.ns9:warning: Before configuring any system to be an LDAP client, ensure that a working LDAP server is present on the network.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure LDAP Client to Use TLS For All Transactions
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Configure LDAP to enforce TLS use. First, edit the file /etc/ldap.conf, and add or correct the following lines: ssl start_tls Then review the LDAP server and ensure TLS has been configured.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The ssl directive specifies whether to use ssl or not. If not specified it will default to no. It should be set to start_tls rather than doing LDAP over SSL.
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: if [ "$(cat /etc/ldap.conf | grep -c '^ssl ')" = "0" ]; then echo "ssl start_tls" | tee -a /etc/ldap.conf &>/dev/null else sed -i 's/^ssl .*/ssl start_tls/' /etc/ldap.conf fi if [ "$(cat /etc/ldap.conf | grep -c '^tls_ciphers ')" = "0" ]; then echo "tls_ciphers TLSv1" | tee -a /etc/ldap.conf &>/dev/null else sed -i 's/^tls_ciphers .*/tls_ciphers TLSv1/' /etc/ldap.conf fi

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To ensure LDAP is configured to use TLS for all transactions, run the following command: $ grep start_tls /etc/ldap.conf

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure Certificate Directives for LDAP Use of TLS
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Ensure a copy of a trusted CA certificate has been placed in the file /etc/pki/tls/CA/cacert.pem. Configure LDAP to enforce TLS use and to trust certificates signed by that CA. First, edit the file /etc/ldap.conf, and add or correct either of the following lines: tls_cert /etc/pki/tls/CA or tls_cert /etc/pki/tls/CA/cacert.pem
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: LDAP can be used to provide user authentication and account information, which are vital to system security. Communication between an LDAP server and a host using LDAP requires authentication.

ns9:check-export.export-name: there is no output, or the lines are commented out

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To ensure TLS is configured with trust certificates, run the following command: # grep tls_cert /etc/ldap.conf

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure Certificate Trust Validation
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Ensure LDAP server connections have a valid trust path. Configure LDAP to enforce validation of LDAP server certificates for trust. First, edit the file /etc/ldap.conf, and add or correct the following line: tls_checkpeer yes
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The NSS LDAP service provides user mappings which are a vital component of system security. Communication between an LDAP server and a host using LDAP for NSS require authentication.
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: if [ $(cat /etc/ldap.conf | grep -c "^tls_checkpeer") = "0" ]; then echo "tls_checkpeer yes" | tee -a /etc/ldap.conf &>/dev/null else sed -i 's/^tls_checkpeer.*/tls_checkpeer yes/' /etc/ldap.conf fi

ns9:check-export.export-name: there is no output, or the lines are commented out

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To ensure TLS is configured to check for trusted certificates, run the following command: # grep tls_checkpeer /etc/ldap.conf

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure Certificate Revocation Validation
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Ensure LDAP server connections have a valid certificate that is not revoked. Configure LDAP to enforce validation of LDAP server certificates for revocation. First, edit the file /etc/ldap.conf, and add or correct the following line: tls_crlcheck all
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: LDAP can be used to provide user authentication and account information, which are vital to system security. Communication between an LDAP server and a host using LDAP requires authentication.
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: if [ $(cat /etc/ldap.conf | grep -c "^tls_crlcheck") = "0" ]; then echo "tls_crlcheck all" | tee -a /etc/ldap.conf &>/dev/null else sed -i 's/^tls_crlcheck.*/tls_crlcheck all/' /etc/ldap.conf fi

ns9:check-export.export-name: there is no output, or the lines are commented out

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To ensure TLS is configured to check for revoked certificates, run the following command: # grep tls_crlcheck /etc/ldap.conf

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: LDAP Passwords Are Stored In Clear Text
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Ensure the LDAP configuration does not include any passwords stored in clear text. Edit the file /etc/ldap.conf, and remove any lines that include the bindpw directive.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The authentication of automated LDAP connections between systems must not use passwords since more secure methods are available, such as PKI and Kerberos. Additionally, the storage of unencrypted passwords on the system is not permitted.

ns9:check-export.export-name: there is no output, or the lines are commented out

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To ensure no passwords are stored in clear text, run the following command: # grep bindpw /etc/ldap.conf

ns9:Group.ns9:title: NFS and RPC
ns9:Group.ns9:description: The Network File System is a popular distributed filesystem for the Unix environment, and is very widely deployed. This section discusses the circumstances under which it is possible to disable NFS and its dependencies, and then details steps which should be taken to secure NFS's configuration. This section is relevant to machines operating as NFS clients, as well as to those operating as NFS servers.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Disable All NFS Services if Possible
ns9:Group.ns9:description: If there is not a reason for the system to operate as either an NFS client or an NFS server, follow all instructions in this section to disable subsystems required by NFS.
ns9:Group.ns9:warning: The steps in this section will prevent a machine from operating as either an NFS client or an NFS server. Only perform these steps on machines which do not need NFS at all.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Remove Services Used Only by NFS
ns9:Group.ns9:description:
If NFS is not needed, remove the NFS client daemons portmap and rpcbind.
All of these daemons run with elevated privileges, and many listen for network connections. If they are not needed, they should be disabled to improve system security posture.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Remove portmap and rpcbind Packages
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: The portmap and rpcbind packages can be uninstalled with the following command: # yum erase portmap rpcbind

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: Run the following command to determine if the portmap package is installed: # rpm -q portmap

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Disable Services Used Only by NFS
ns9:Group.ns9:description:
If NFS is not needed, disable the NFS client daemons nfslock, rpcgssd, and rpcidmapd.
All of these daemons run with elevated privileges, and many listen for network connections. If they are not needed, they should be disabled to improve system security posture.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Disable portmap and rpcbind Services
ns9:Rule.ns9:description:
The rpcbind service increase the attack surface of the system and should only be used when needed. The rpcbind service are used by a variety of services using Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs).
The rpcbind service can be disabled with the following command: # chkconfig rpcbind off

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Configure All Machines which Use NFS
ns9:Group.ns9:description: The steps in this section are appropriate for all machines which run NFS, whether they operate as clients or as servers.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Configure NFS Clients
ns9:Group.ns9:description: The steps in this section are appropriate for machines which operate as NFS clients.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Mount Remote Filesystems with nosuid
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Add the nosuid option to the fourth column of /etc/fstab for the line which controls mounting of any NFS mounts.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: NFS mounts should not present suid binaries to users. Only vendor-supplied suid executables should be installed to their default location on the local filesystem.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To verify the nosuid option is configured for all NFS mounts, run the following command: $ mount | grep nfs All NFS mounts should show the nosuid setting in parentheses. This is not applicable if NFS is not implemented.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Configure NFS Servers
ns9:Group.ns9:description: The steps in this section are appropriate for machines which operate as NFS servers.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Specify UID and GID for Anonymous NFS Connections
ns9:Rule.ns9:description:
To specify the UID and GID for remote root users, edit the /etc/exports file and add the following for each export:
anonuid=-1 anongid=-1
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Specifying the anonymous UID and GID as -1 ensures that the remote root user is mapped to a local account which has no permissions on the system.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: All Exports Must Define Allowed Targets
ns9:Rule.ns9:description:
When configuring NFS exports, ensure that each export line in /etc/exports contains a list of hosts which are allowed to access that export. If no hosts are specified on an export line, then that export is available to any remote host which requests it. All lines of the exports file should specify the hosts (or subnets, if needed) which are allowed to access the exported directory, so that unknown or remote hosts will be denied.
Authorized hosts can be specified in several different formats:
Name or alias that is recognized by the resolver
Fully qualified domain name
IP address
IP subnets in the format address/netmask or address/CIDR
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The NFS access option limits user access to the specified level. This assists in protecting exported file systems. If access is not restricted, unauthorized hosts may be able to access the system's NFS exports.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Use Root-Squashing on All Exports
ns9:Rule.ns9:description:
If a filesystem is exported using root squashing, requests from root on the client are considered to be unprivileged (mapped to a user such as nobody). This provides some mild protection against remote abuse of an NFS server. Root squashing is enabled by default, and should not be disabled.
Ensure that no line in /etc/exports contains the option no_root_squash.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: If the NFS server allows root access to local file systems from remote hosts, this access could be used to compromise the system.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Ensure Insecure File Locking is Not Allowed
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: By default the NFS server requires secure file-lock requests, which require credentials from the client in order to lock a file. Most NFS clients send credentials with file lock requests, however, there are a few clients that do not send credentials when requesting a file-lock, allowing the client to only be able to lock world-readable files. To get around this, the insecure_locks option can be used so these clients can access the desired export. This poses a security risk by potentially allowing the client access to data for which it does not have authorization. Remove any instances of the insecure_locks option from the file /etc/exports.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Allowing insecure file locking could allow for sensitive data to be viewed or edited by an unauthorized user.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To verify insecure file locking has been disabled, run the following command: # grep insecure_locks /etc/exports

ns9:Group.ns9:title: FTP Server
ns9:Group.ns9:description:
FTP is a common method for allowing remote access to files. Like telnet, the FTP protocol is unencrypted, which means that passwords and other data transmitted during the session can be captured and that the session is vulnerable to hijacking. Therefore, running the FTP server software is not recommended.
However, there are some FTP server configurations which may be appropriate for some environments, particularly those which allow only read-only anonymous access as a means of downloading data available to the public.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Disable Unencrypted FTP Services
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: The vsftpd service can be disabled with the following command: # chkconfig vsftpd off
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Running unencrypted FTP server software provides a network-based avenue of attack, and should be disabled if not needed. Furthermore, the FTP protocol is unencrypted and creates a risk of compromising sensitive information.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content:
To check that the vsftpd service is disabled in system boot configuration, run the following command: # chkconfig vsftpd --list Output should indicate the vsftpd service has either not been installed, or has been disabled at all runlevels, as shown in the example below: # chkconfig vsftpd --list vsftpd 0:off 1:off 2:off 3:off 4:off 5:off 6:off
Run the following command to verify vsftpd is disabled through current runtime configuration: # service vsftpd status
If the service is disabled the command will return the following output: vsftpd is stopped

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Enable Logging of All FTP Transactions
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Add or correct the following configuration options within the vsftpd configuration file, located at /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf: xferlog_enable=YES xferlog_std_format=NO log_ftp_protocol=YES
ns9:Rule.ns9:warning: If verbose logging to vsftpd.log is done, sparse logging of downloads to /var/log/xferlog will not also occur. However, the information about what files were downloaded is included in the information logged to vsftpd.log
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: To trace malicious activity facilitated by the FTP service, it must be configured to ensure that all commands sent to the FTP server are logged using the verbose vsftpd log format. The default vsftpd log file is /var/log/vsftpd.log.
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: if [ -e /etc/xinetd.d/gssftp ]; then if [ "$(grep server_args /etc/xinetd.d/gssftp | grep -c " -l")" = "0" ]; then sed -i "/server_args/s/$/ -l/" /etc/xinetd.d/gssftp fi fi if [ -e /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf ]; then if [ "$(grep -ic "^xferlog_enable=yes" /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf)" = "0" ]; then sed -i "s/xferlog_enable.*/xferlog_enable=yes/" /etc/xinetd.d/gssftp fi fi

ns9:check-export.export-name: xferlog_enable is missing, or is not set to yes

ns9:check.ns9:check-content:
Find if logging is applied to the FTP daemon.
Procedures:
If vsftpd is started by xinetd the following command will indicate the xinetd.d startup file: # grep vsftpd /etc/xinetd.d/* # grep server_args vsftpd xinetd.d startup file This will indicate the vsftpd config file used when starting through xinetd. If the server_args line is missing or does not include the vsftpd configuration file, then the default config file (/etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf) is used. # grep xferlog_enable vsftpd config file

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: FTP Umask Must Be 077.
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: All FTP users must have a default umask of 077.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The umask controls the default access mode assigned to newly created files. An umask of 077 limits new files to mode 700 or less permissive. Although umask is stored as a 4-digit number, the first digit representing special access modes is typically ignored or required to be zero (0).
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: if [ "$(rpm -q krb5-workstation &>/dev/null; echo $?)" = "0" ]; then if [ "$(grep server_args /etc/xinetd.d/gssftp | grep -v "#" | grep -c "\-u 077")" = "0" ]; then sed -i '/server_args/s/$/ -u 077/' /etc/xinetd.d/gssftp fi fi if [ "$(rpm -q vsftpd &>/dev/null; echo $?)" = "0" ]; then if [ "$(grep -c local_umask /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf)" = "0" ]; then echo "local_umask=077" >> /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf else sed -i '/local_umask/s/=.*/=077/' /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf fi if [ "$(grep -c anon_umask /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf)" = "0" ]; then echo "anon_umask=077" >> /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf else sed -i '/anon_umask/s/=.*/=077/' /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf fi fi

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Ftpusers File Contains Users
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: The ftpusers file must contain account names not allowed to use FTP.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The ftpusers file contains a list of accounts not allowed to use FTP to transfer files. If the file does not contain the names of all accounts not authorized to use FTP, then unauthorized use of FTP may take place.
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: SYS_USER=$(cat /etc/passwd | while read entry; do if [ "$(echo ${entry} | cut -d: -f3)" -lt "500" ]; then echo ${entry} | cut -d: -f1 ; fi; done) if [ "$(rpm -q krb5-workstation &>/dev/null; echo $?)" = "0" ]; then if [ ! -e /etc/ftpusers ]; then >/etc/ftpusers chmod 0640 /etc/ftpusers chown root:root /etc/ftpusers fi for USER in `echo $SYS_USER`; do if [ $(grep -c "^${USER}$" /etc/ftpusers) = 0 ]; then echo ${USER} | tee -a /etc/ftpusers &>/dev/null fi done fi if [ "$(rpm -q vsftpd &>/dev/null; echo $?)" = "0" ]; then if [ ! -e /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers ]; then >/etc/vsftpd/ftpusers chmod 0640 /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers chown root:root /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers fi for USER in `echo $SYS_USER`; do if [ $(grep -c "^${USER}$" /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers) = 0 ]; then echo ${USER} | tee -a /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers &>/dev/null fi done fi

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Ftpusers File Exists
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: The ftpusers file must exist.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The ftpusers file contains a list of accounts not allowed to use FTP to transfer files. If this file does not exist, then unauthorized accounts can utilize FTP.
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: SYS_USER=$(cat /etc/passwd | while read entry; do if [ "$(echo ${entry} | cut -d: -f3)" -lt "500" ]; then echo ${entry} | cut -d: -f1 ; fi; done) if [ "$(rpm -q krb5-workstation &>/dev/null; echo $?)" = "0" ]; then if [ ! -e /etc/ftpusers ]; then >/etc/ftpusers chmod 0640 /etc/ftpusers chown root:root /etc/ftpusers fi for USER in `echo $SYS_USER`; do if [ $(grep -c "^${USER}$" /etc/ftpusers) = 0 ]; then echo ${USER} | tee -a /etc/ftpusers &>/dev/null fi done fi if [ "$(rpm -q vsftpd &>/dev/null; echo $?)" = "0" ]; then if [ ! -e /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers ]; then >/etc/vsftpd/ftpusers chmod 0640 /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers chown root:root /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers fi for USER in `echo $SYS_USER`; do if [ $(grep -c "^${USER}$" /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers) = 0 ]; then echo ${USER} | tee -a /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers &>/dev/null fi done fi

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: FTP User Has Shell
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Anonymous FTP accounts must not have a functional shell.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: If an anonymous FTP account has been configured to use a functional shell, attackers could gain access to the shell if the account is compromised.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: TFTP User Has Shell
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: The TFTP daemon must be configured to vendor specifications, including a dedicated TFTP user account, a non-login shell such as /bin/false, and a home directory owned by the TFTP user.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: If TFTP has a valid shell, it increases the likelihood someone could log on to the TFTP account and compromise the system.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Samba(SMB) Microsoft Windows File Sharing Server
ns9:Group.ns9:description: When properly configured, the Samba service allows Linux machines to provide file and print sharing to Microsoft Windows machines. There are two software packages that provide Samba support. The first, samba-client, provides a series of command line tools that enable a client machine to access Samba shares. The second, simply labeled samba, provides the Samba service. It is this second package that allows a Linux machine to act as an Active Directory server, a domain controller, or as a domain member. Only the samba-client package is installed by default.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Remove Samba if Possible
ns9:Group.ns9:description: The Samba server must not be installed unless it provides an operational need.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Remove samba and samba3x Packages
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: The samba and samba3x packages can be uninstalled with the following command: # yum erase samba samba3x

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: Run the following command to determine if the samba package is installed: # rpm -q samba

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Configure Samba if Necessary
ns9:Group.ns9:description: All settings for the Samba daemon can be found in /etc/samba/smb.conf. Settings are divided between a [global] configuration section and a series of user created share definition sections meant to describe file or print shares on the system. By default, Samba will operate in user mode and allow client machines to access local home directories and printers. It is recommended that these settings be changed or that additional limitations be set in place.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Samba Web Administration Tool Must Be Restricted
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: The Samba Web Administration Tool (SWAT) must be restricted to the local host or require SSL.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: SWAT is a tool used to configure Samba. It modifies Samba configuration, which can impact system security, and must be protected from unauthorized access. SWAT authentication may involve the root password, which must be protected by encryption when traversing the network. Restricting access to the local host allows for the use of SSH TCP forwarding, if configured, or administration by a web browser on the local system.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure hosts Option
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Samba increases the attack surface of the system and must be restricted to communicate only with systems requiring access.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Specifying the anonymous UID and GID as -1 ensures that the remote root user is mapped to a local account which has no permissions on the system.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure security Option
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Samba share authentication does not provide for individual user identification and must not be used.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Specifying the anonymous UID and GID as -1 ensures that the remote root user is mapped to a local account which has no permissions on the system.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure encrypt passwords Option
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Samba must be configured to use encrypted passwords.
ns9:Rule.ns9:fix: if [ "$(grep -c '^[ |\t]*encrypt passwords' /etc/samba/smb.conf)" = "0" ]; then sed -i 's/\(^\[global\]$\)/\1\n\n\tencrypt passwords = yes/' /etc/samba/smb.conf else sed -i '/^[#|;]/!s/\(encrypt passwords =\).*/\1 yes/g' /etc/samba/smb.conf fi

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure guest ok Option
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Guest access to shares permits anonymous access and is not permitted.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: SNMP Server
ns9:Group.ns9:description: The Simple Network Management Protocol allows administrators to monitor the state of network devices, including computers. Older versions of SNMP were well-known for weak security, such as plaintext transmission of the community string (used for authentication) and usage of easily-guessable choices for the community string.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Configure SNMP Server
ns9:Group.ns9:description:
If it is necessary to run the snmpd agent on the system, some best practices should be followed to minimize the security risk from the installation. The multiple security models implemented by SNMP cannot be fully covered here so only the following general configuration advice can be offered:
use only SNMP version 3 security models and enable the use of authentication and encryption
write access to the MIB (Management Information Base) should be allowed only if necessary
all access to the MIB should be restricted following a principle of least privilege
network access should be limited to the maximum extent possible including restricting to expected network addresses both in the configuration files and in the system firewall rules
ensure SNMP agents send traps only to, and accept SNMP queries only from, authorized management stations
ensure that permissions on the snmpd.conf configuration file (by default, in /etc/snmp) are 640 or more restrictive
ensure that any MIB files' permissions are also 640 or more restrictive

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Configure SNMP Service to Use Only SNMPv3 or Newer
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Edit /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf, removing any references to v1, v2c, or com2sec. Upon doing that, restart the SNMP service: # service snmpd restart
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Earlier versions of SNMP are considered insecure, as they potentially allow unauthorized access to detailed system management information.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To ensure only SNMPv3 or newer is used, run the following command: # grep 'v1\|v2c\|community\|com2sec' /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf | grep -v "^#" There should be no output.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Ensure Default Password Is Not Used
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Edit /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf, remove default community strings public, private, snmp-trap, password. Upon doing that, restart the SNMP service: # service snmpd restart
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Presence of the default SNMP password enables querying of different system aspects and could result in unauthorized knowledge of the system.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To ensure the default password is not set, run the following command: # grep -v "^#" /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf| grep 'public\|private\|snmp-trap\|password' There should be no output.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Ensure Approved Hash Is Used
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Edit /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf, ensure every line beginning with createUser includes SHA, similar to the following: # createUser myuser SHA -l 0x0001020304050607080900010203040506070809 AES -l 0x00010203040506070809000102030405 Upon doing that, restart the SNMP service: # service snmpd restart
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The SNMP service must use SHA-1 or a FIPS 140-2 approved successor for authentication and integrity.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To ensure SHA is used for SNMPv3 users, run the following command: # grep -v '^#' /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf | grep -i createUser | grep -vi SHA There should be no output.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Ensure Approved Encryption Is Used
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Edit /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf, ensure every line beginning with createUser includes AES, similar to the following: # createUser myuser SHA -l 0x0001020304050607080900010203040506070809 AES -l 0x00010203040506070809000102030405 Upon doing that, restart the SNMP service: # service snmpd restart
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The SNMP service must use AES or a FIPS 140-2 approved successor algorithm for protecting the privacy of communications.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: To ensure AES is used for SNMPv3 users, run the following command: # grep -v '^#' /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf | grep -i createUser | grep -vi AES There should be no output.

ns9:Group.ns9:title: Documentation to Support DISA OS SRG Mapping
ns9:Group.ns9:description: These groups exist to document how the Red Hat Enterprise Linux product meets (or does not meet) requirements listed in the DISA OS SRG, for those cases where Groups or Rules elsewhere in scap-security-guide do not clearly relate.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Product Meets this Requirement
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: This requirement is a permanent not a finding. No fix is required.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Red Hat Enterprise Linux meets this requirement through design and implementation.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: RHEL6 supports this requirement and cannot be configured to be out of compliance. This is a permanent not a finding.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Product Meets this Requirement
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: This requirement is a permanent not a finding. No fix is required.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux audit system meets this requirement through design and implementation.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: The RHEL6 auditing system supports this requirement and cannot be configured to be out of compliance. Every audit record in RHEL includes a timestamp, the operation attempted, success or failure of the operation, the subject involved (executable/process), the object involved (file/path), and security labels for the subject and object. It also includes the ability to label events with custom key labels. The auditing system centralizes the recording of audit events for the entire system and includes reduction (ausearch), reporting (aureport), and real-time response (audispd) facilities. This is a permanent not a finding.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Product Meets this Requirement
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: This requirement is a permanent not a finding. No fix is required.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: Red Hat Enterprise Linux meets this requirement through design and implementation.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: RHEL6 supports this requirement and cannot be configured to be out of compliance. This is a permanent not a finding.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Guidance Does Not Meet this Requirement Due to Impracticality or Scope
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: This requirement is NA. No fix is required.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The guidance does not meet this requirement. The requirement is impractical or out of scope.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: RHEL6 cannot support this requirement without assistance from an external application, policy, or service. This requirement is NA.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Implementation of the Requirement is Not Supported
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: This requirement is a permanent finding and cannot be fixed. An appropriate mitigation for the system must be implemented but this finding cannot be considered fixed.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: RHEL6 does not support this requirement.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: This is a permanent finding.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: Guidance Does Not Meet this Requirement Due to Impracticality or Scope
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: This requirement is NA. No fix is required.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: The guidance does not meet this requirement. The requirement is impractical or out of scope.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content: RHEL6 cannot support this requirement without assistance from an external application, policy, or service. This requirement is NA.

ns9:Rule.ns9:title: A process for prompt installation of OS updates must exist.
ns9:Rule.ns9:description: Procedures to promptly apply software updates must be established and executed. The Red Hat operating system provides support for automating such a process, by running the yum program through a cron job or by managing the system and its packages through the Red Hat Network or a Satellite Server.
ns9:Rule.ns9:rationale: This is a manual inquiry about update procedure.

ns9:check.ns9:check-content:
Ask an administrator if a process exists to promptly and automatically apply OS software updates. If such a process does not exist, this is a finding.
If the OS update process limits automatic updates of software packages, where such updates would impede normal system operation, to scheduled maintenance windows, but still within IAVM-dictated timeframes, this is not a finding.
